title: Unsafe Blocking or Fallible Cleanup in Drop/Destructor
pattern: Placing fallible, blocking, or asynchronous network/disk cleanup operations (such as flushing writes or closing connections) inside a type's destructor (`Drop` implementation).
why_bad: Destructors in compiled languages like Rust cannot safely propagate errors to the caller or register with asynchronous runtimes easily. If they fail, they are forced to either panic (causing double-panics during unwinding) or silently swallow errors.
detection: A `Drop` or destructor implementation that performs I/O operations, blocks on locks, or flushes buffers without fallback error-handling.
counterexample: Simple in-memory memory deallocations or non-blocking, infallible file closures.
fix: Expose an explicit, fallible, consuming shutdown method (e.g., `fn close(self) -> Result<(), Error>`), leaving `Drop` as a silent, best-effort fallback.
source: Jon Gjengset, *Rust for Rustaceans*, Chapter 9 / passage [445].
